title: THE CROWD FELT THE FIRE… BUT WAS GOD EVEN IN THE ROOM?
paragraphs: THE CROWD FELT THE FIRE… BUT WAS GOD EVEN IN THE ROOM?
Are Christians Confusing Charisma With the Anointing of God? The Dangerous Difference Between a Powerful Personality and the Presence of the Holy Spirit.
The preacher stepped onto the platform.
Before he even opened his Bible, the atmosphere changed.
The music swelled. The lights dimmed. Thousands of hands went up. People began shouting, crying, trembling. Every sentence seemed to ignite another wave of emotion.
Someone whispered, “You can feel the anointing on this man.”
Another declared, “God is really moving tonight!”
And perhaps He was.
But somewhere in that crowded room was a question nobody wanted to ask.
What if the crowd was responding to the man more than surrendering to Jesus?
What if the tears were real, the emotions were overwhelming, the message was beautifully delivered… but the people walked away more impressed with the preacher than transformed by the Gospel?
And what if the most dangerous thing happening in some churches today is not the absence of spiritual excitement, but our growing inability to distinguish excitement from the work of the Holy Spirit?
Please don't misunderstand me.
God can move powerfully through passionate preaching. He can use a commanding voice, an unforgettable testimony, beautiful music, and even an emotionally charged atmosphere to awaken hearts.
The Holy Spirit is not afraid of human emotion.
But neither is human emotion proof that the Holy Spirit is moving.
And that distinction matters more than many of us realize.
Because you can leave a church service shaking without leaving your sin.
You can cry during worship and still refuse to forgive the person who hurt you.
You can fall to your knees in a crowded sanctuary and stand up with the same pride, bitterness, dishonesty, and secret compromises you brought inside.
You can be moved by a sermon without being moved toward repentance.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility of all…
You can become deeply attached to a preacher while remaining spiritually distant from the Christ he is supposed to proclaim.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Not because every charismatic preacher is false.
Not because every emotional worship service is manufactured.
And certainly not because the Holy Spirit has stopped working through extraordinary people.
But because Scripture repeatedly warns us that spiritual appearances and spiritual reality are not always the same thing.
Jesus said something in Matthew 7:22–23 that should make every preacher, worship leader, ministry founder, and church member examine their heart.
Many would come to Him claiming to have prophesied, cast out demons, and performed mighty works in His name.
Yet Jesus would declare that He never knew them.
Think about that.
These were not people who merely claimed to be good public speakers.
They appealed to spectacular religious activity.
They spoke of works that appeared spiritually impressive.
And still, Jesus exposed the terrifying possibility of religious activity without a genuine relationship with Him.
The Greek text of Matthew 7:23 includes the words:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”

The word egnōn comes from ginōskō, meaning “to know.” In this context, Jesus is not suggesting that He lacked information about these people. He is denying that they belonged to Him in the saving relationship they presumed to possess.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say, “Your sermons were not entertaining enough.”
He did not say, “Your gatherings were not large enough.”
He did not say, “Your ministry lacked public influence.”
The issue was deeper.
They could point to extraordinary works, but they could not establish genuine belonging to Christ.

And if outwardly impressive religious works cannot, by themselves, establish that someone belongs to Jesus, why have we allowed stage presence, eloquence, popularity, and emotional intensity to become our measurements of spiritual authority?
Somewhere along the way, we began confusing a powerful delivery with a powerful life.
We started assuming that because someone can command a room, they must be submitted to God.
Because they can quote Scripture without looking down, they must be living under Scripture when nobody is watching.
Because they can make thousands cry, they must be faithfully shepherding the souls entrusted to them.
But a gift can attract attention while character reveals what someone does with that attention.
And that is where the difference between charisma and anointing becomes essential.
The English word charisma commonly refers to compelling personal charm, magnetism, or influence.
Interestingly, the New Testament also uses the Greek word χάρισμα (charisma), but with a different meaning.
In passages such as Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4, charisma refers to a graciously given gift.
It comes from the same word family as χάρις (charis), meaning grace.
That distinction matters.
Modern personality charisma and biblical spiritual gifts are not interchangeable concepts.
A person may have extraordinary communication skills without possessing mature Christian character.
And someone may receive a genuine spiritual gift without that gift being evidence that every aspect of their life is pleasing to God.
Paul addressed spiritual gifts extensively in 1 Corinthians 12–14.
But between those chapters stands something remarkable.
First Corinthians 13.
Love.
Not celebrity.
Not influence.
Not emotional spectacle.
Love.
Paul declares that even extraordinary speech, knowledge, faith, and sacrifice amount to nothing spiritually if love is absent.
The church at Corinth had spiritual gifts, yet Paul also confronted jealousy, divisions, pride, disorder, and immaturity among them.
Apparently, giftedness and maturity are not identical.
A person can be gifted and still need serious correction.
A congregation can experience remarkable spiritual activity and still require repentance.
And a ministry can appear successful in the eyes of the world while carrying unresolved problems that demand biblical accountability.
This is why the word anointing deserves careful handling.
In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word מָשַׁח (māšaḥ) means “to anoint,” commonly referring to the application of oil in setting someone apart for a particular office or purpose.
From this word family comes מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ), meaning “anointed one,” the source of the title Messiah.
In the New Testament, χρίω (chriō) means “to anoint,” and Χριστός (Christos) means “Anointed One,” the title we translate as Christ.
Jesus is the Messiah, the Christ, the Anointed One.
In Luke 4:18, Jesus reads from Isaiah and announces that the Spirit of the Lord is upon Him because He has been anointed to proclaim good news.
His ministry is not built around personal celebrity.
It reveals the Father's saving purpose.
He brings good news to the poor, freedom to captives, sight to the blind, and liberty to the oppressed.
The Anointed One comes to save.
And that raises a question we cannot afford to ignore.
If Jesus is the center of God's saving work, why do some of our ministries seem to collapse emotionally whenever the human personality at the center is questioned?
Why does examining a preacher's teaching sometimes feel, to his followers, like attacking God Himself?
Why do sincere believers sometimes defend a leader's reputation more fiercely than they defend the truth of Scripture?
Why do people feel permitted to question politicians, doctors, teachers, and business executives, yet become afraid to ask reasonable questions about someone who claims to speak for God?
The Bible never teaches that spiritual leadership places a person beyond examination.
Quite the opposite.
First Thessalonians 5:19–21 tells believers not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecies, but to test everything and hold fast to what is good.
Notice the balance.
Do not despise genuine spiritual activity.
But do not surrender discernment.
The Greek expression πάντα δὲ δοκιμάζετε (panta de dokimazete) means, in context, “but test everything.”
The verb dokimazō carries the sense of examining or testing to determine what is genuine or approved.
Biblical discernment is not cynicism.
It is not automatically accusing every passionate preacher of deception.
It is not treating miracles as impossible or emotional worship as inherently suspicious.
It is refusing to confuse spiritual authenticity with spiritual appearance.
And sometimes, the most loving thing you can do for a church is ask whether its practices agree with the Word of God.
Remember the believers in Berea?
Acts 17:11 commends them because they received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to see whether what Paul taught was true.
Paul was an apostle.
Yet examining his teaching against Scripture was described positively.
If the Bereans could examine Paul's message, why should any modern preacher expect unquestioning loyalty?
A faithful minister should welcome the Bible being opened.
Because a faithful minister knows the congregation belongs to Jesus.
Not to him.
Not to his family.
Not to his organization.
Not to his platform.
To Jesus.
And that brings us to something many Christians have experienced but rarely know how to explain.
Have you ever attended a service where everything felt extraordinary?
The music was beautiful.
The preacher was captivating.
The atmosphere was intense.
You went home saying, “That was powerful.”
But a week later, you could remember the preacher's jokes, his dramatic stories, and the moment the congregation erupted…
Yet you struggled to remember what the passage actually taught about Christ.
You remembered how you felt.
But not what God said.
That experience alone does not prove the service was spiritually empty. Human memory is imperfect, and God may be working in ways we cannot immediately measure.
Still, it is worth asking what our gatherings consistently train us to value.
Are we learning to understand Scripture?
Are we growing in repentance, prayer, holiness, mercy, generosity, and love?
Are we becoming more faithful spouses, parents, children, neighbors, and servants?
Are we learning to endure suffering without abandoning Christ?
Or are we becoming dependent on the next emotional high?
Because spiritual growth cannot be sustained by atmosphere alone.
There will be mornings when the worship music does not move you.
Days when prayer feels difficult.
Seasons when the church is small, the preacher is ordinary, the room is quiet, and your heart is exhausted.
And on those days, you need something stronger than the memory of an exciting service.
You need the truth of the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
You need a Savior who remains faithful when your emotions are inconsistent.
You need grace that does not disappear when the music stops.
You need the Gospel.
The apostle Paul understood this.
In 1 Corinthians 2:1–5, he explained that he did not approach the Corinthians relying on lofty speech or human wisdom.
He resolved to know Jesus Christ and Him crucified.
Paul was not condemning careful communication or persuasive reasoning. Elsewhere, Scripture shows him reasoning, explaining, and persuading.
He was rejecting dependence on worldly rhetorical impressiveness as the foundation of faith.
His concern was that their faith would rest not on human wisdom but on God's power.
There is an enormous difference between using communication skills to make the Gospel understandable and using the Gospel to make yourself indispensable.
One serves Christ.
The other risks making Christ's people dependent on a personality.
And we need to be careful here.
A quiet preacher is not automatically anointed.
A loud preacher is not automatically carnal.
A large church is not automatically compromised.
A small church is not automatically faithful.
Tears do not prove repentance, but neither does the absence of tears prove spiritual coldness.
God works through different personalities, cultures, traditions, and styles.
The question is not whether a preacher is exciting.
The question is whether he is faithful.
Does he handle Scripture responsibly?
Does he proclaim the biblical Gospel?
Does he acknowledge sin without withholding the hope of grace?
Does he point people toward Jesus rather than making himself the center of their spiritual identity?
Does his conduct demonstrate humility and accountability?
Does he treat people with dignity, especially those who have little influence or money?
Can he be corrected?
Can he apologize?
Can he admit when he has been wrong?
And when serious allegations arise, does he welcome appropriate, independent examination rather than using spiritual language to silence legitimate concerns?
These questions matter because Scripture gives moral qualifications for church leaders.
First Timothy 3 and Titus 1 emphasize character, self-control, faithfulness, sound teaching, and a respectable life.
The Bible does not say that an overseer must possess extraordinary stage presence.
It says he must be above reproach.
Not sinless.
But genuinely accountable, faithful, and qualified.
Jesus also warned in Matthew 7:15–20 that false prophets must be recognized by their fruits.
The Greek word καρπός (karpos) means “fruit.”
In that passage, the image concerns what a person's life and ministry produce and reveal.
Fruit is not simply the number of followers someone accumulates.
It is not the number of people who purchase their books.
It is not how many invitations they receive to speak.
Public reach may create opportunities for good, but it is not a reliable substitute for biblical faithfulness.
And Galatians 5:22–23 gives us a picture of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Imagine if Christians became as attentive to those qualities as we are to dramatic testimonies and viral preaching clips.
Imagine asking not merely, “How powerful was his sermon?”
But, “How does he treat his family? His staff? The vulnerable? The person who disagrees with him?”
Imagine evaluating ministries not only by the crowds they gather, but by whether they help people become more faithful disciples of Jesus.
Something would change.
Perhaps fewer personalities would become untouchable.
Perhaps more wounded people would be heard.
Perhaps gifted ministers would receive correction before private compromises became public disasters.
And perhaps ordinary, faithful pastors who have never gone viral would finally receive the appreciation they deserve.
Because somewhere tonight, a pastor will preach to thirty people in a modest building.
There will be no sophisticated lighting.
No dramatic entrance.
No trending clips.
He may stumble over a sentence.
His voice may shake.
He may spend the afternoon visiting someone in the hospital, then return home exhausted before preparing for Sunday.
And when he opens his Bible, he will faithfully explain the Word of God.
He will call sinners to repentance.
He will remind weary believers of the mercy of Christ.
He will pray for families whose names the internet will never know.
And heaven's evaluation of his faithfulness is not determined by his inability to fill a stadium.
Meanwhile, another preacher may stand before thousands and faithfully proclaim the same Jesus with extraordinary skill and genuine humility.
Both can serve God.
Both can be used by the Spirit.
The issue has never been audience size.
The issue is whether the messenger is serving the message, or the message has become a tool for magnifying the messenger.
And before we make this entirely about preachers, we need to confront a painful truth.
Sometimes the congregation participates in creating the very celebrity culture it later condemns.
We demand excitement.
We reward spectacle.
We treat faithful exposition as boring if it does not produce an immediate emotional reaction.
We sometimes prefer the preacher who tells us we are destined for greatness over the preacher who lovingly confronts the sin destroying our homes.
We want encouragement without correction.
Victory without surrender.
Blessing without obedience.
A crown without a cross.
Second Timothy 4:3–4 warns that a time will come when people will not endure sound teaching, but will accumulate teachers who suit their own desires.
That warning is not permission to label everyone who disagrees with us a false teacher.
It is a call to examine what we ourselves want to hear.
Because sometimes we are not deceived simply because someone is persuasive.
Sometimes we are vulnerable because their message tells us exactly what our flesh wants to believe.
And this is where the article stops being about someone else.
What if you have been more excited about being noticed in church than becoming holy before God?
What if you have been chasing prophetic declarations while neglecting the plain commands of Scripture?
What if you have memorized your favorite preacher's catchphrases but have not opened your Bible in weeks?
What if you have been calling every emotional experience an encounter with God, while avoiding the difficult obedience He has already made clear?
What if you love hearing about breakthrough, but resist hearing about repentance?
I ask these questions with no claim of superiority.
Because all of us can become fascinated by appearances.
All of us can mistake spiritual activity for spiritual intimacy.
All of us can drift into seeking the gifts of God while neglecting communion with the Giver.
And the answer is not to become suspicious of everything beautiful, emotional, or extraordinary.
The answer is to return to Jesus.
Look at Him.
The One who could command storms did not build His ministry around demanding applause.
The One who multiplied bread refused to reduce His mission to satisfying crowds.
The One who possessed all authority washed His disciples' feet.
The One who was truly without sin willingly endured humiliation.
The One worthy of every crown wore thorns.
And the One who could have summoned heavenly deliverance submitted Himself to the cross to accomplish our redemption.
Philippians 2:5–11 calls believers to embrace the mind of Christ, who humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
The way of Jesus is not self-exaltation disguised as ministry.
It is humble obedience to the Father.
And here is the scandal that becomes grace.
We have often celebrated the impressive while overlooking the faithful.
We have sometimes elevated personalities above accountability.
We have confused emotional intensity with spiritual maturity.
We have wanted to be associated with greatness more than we have wanted to become servants.
Yet Jesus still calls us back.
Not because our discernment has been perfect.
Not because our motives have always been pure.
But because His mercy is greater than the failures we are willing to bring into His light.
The Gospel is not merely a warning against deceptive religion.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
According to 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day.
That is the center.
Not the preacher's personality.
Not the atmosphere.
Not the platform.
The crucified and risen Savior.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and new life.
Maybe you are reading this after being deeply wounded by a church leader you once admired.
Maybe you defended someone for years, only to discover that serious wrongdoing had been hidden behind spiritual language.
Maybe you trusted a ministry so completely that when its leader failed, your faith nearly collapsed with it.
I want you to hear something.
Jesus is not identical to the person who misrepresented Him.
The failure of a spiritual leader is grievous, but it does not overturn the truth of Christ.
You are permitted to grieve.
You are permitted to ask questions.
You are permitted to seek safety, accountability, and justice.
Forgiveness does not require pretending abuse never happened, abandoning appropriate consequences, or immediately restoring someone to a position of authority.
And you do not have to rush your healing to make other people comfortable.
Bring your wounded heart to Jesus.
He is not threatened by the truth.
Maybe, on the other hand, you are a preacher, teacher, worship leader, or ministry worker reading this with an uncomfortable weight in your chest.
You remember when ministry was simple.
When you prayed because you loved God, not because someone might see you.
When you opened Scripture because you were hungry for truth, not because you needed material for your next post.
When serving ten people felt like an honor.
But somewhere along the journey, numbers began to matter too much.
Recognition became intoxicating.
Criticism became unbearable.
And the thought of losing your influence began to frighten you more than the thought of losing your integrity.
If that is you, do not wait for a public collapse before seeking repentance.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Welcome godly accountability.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Step away from responsibilities if serious wrongdoing or disqualifying conduct requires it.
Do not protect a platform at the expense of people's souls.
The mercy of Christ is not an excuse to hide sin.
It is an invitation to bring sin into the light.
And perhaps the greatest freedom you can rediscover is this:
You were never called to be someone's savior.
Jesus already is.
You do not have to manufacture the presence of God.
You do not have to manipulate tears.
You do not have to turn every sermon into a performance.
You do not have to make people dependent on your voice.
Preach Christ faithfully.
Love people genuinely.
Handle Scripture carefully.
Serve without pretending to be more than you are.
And trust the Holy Spirit to accomplish what human charisma never could.
Because no amount of eloquence can regenerate a dead heart.
No lighting arrangement can produce genuine repentance.
No musical crescendo can guarantee holiness.
No personality can replace the saving work of Jesus.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
And the Spirit works through the truth of Christ to draw sinners to Him.
That does not make faithful communication unimportant.
It puts communication in its proper place.
A servant.
Not a savior.
And maybe this is what the church desperately needs to remember in an age when nearly everything can be edited, amplified, branded, and promoted.
The Holy Spirit is not a stage effect.
He is God.
He cannot be reduced to a feeling, a vocal technique, a viral moment, or a leader's reputation.
Jesus described the Spirit in John 16:13–14 as the One who guides into truth and glorifies Christ.
That gives us a deeply important direction for discernment.
Where the Holy Spirit is truly at work, His work is never ultimately in competition with the glory of Jesus.
The Spirit's ministry does not require us to idolize the messenger.
It draws us toward the Son.
And the Son brings us to the Father.
So the next time you hear someone say, “That preacher is so anointed,” do not immediately dismiss them.
But ask a better question.
What do they mean?
Do they mean the preacher communicates with extraordinary skill?
Do they mean the sermon faithfully revealed the meaning of Scripture?
Do they mean people were moved toward repentance, faith, and obedience to Christ?
Do they mean the preacher's life reflects the humility and integrity required of spiritual leadership?
Or do they simply mean the room became emotional?
Those are not the same things.
And distinguishing them may protect both your faith and your church.
When was the last time you left a worship service thinking more about the beauty of Jesus than the brilliance of the person on stage?
When was the last time Scripture corrected you and you welcomed that correction?
When was the last time you obeyed God without needing anyone to notice?
When was the last time you chose the quiet, costly path of faithfulness over the excitement of being seen?
Because the Christian life is not a competition to appear spiritually impressive.
It is a call to follow the Savior who gave Himself for us.
And the deepest evidence of God's transforming work may not always appear in a dramatic public moment.
Sometimes it appears when a husband finally confesses his dishonesty and seeks to rebuild trust.
When a wife chooses to speak truth with grace instead of retaliating in anger.
When a young person turns away from a secret sin and seeks help.
When a believer who has been wronged refuses to surrender to bitterness, even while pursuing appropriate justice.
When a struggling Christian opens the Bible again after months of spiritual exhaustion.
When a pastor admits he was wrong.
When a church protects the vulnerable instead of protecting its image.
When someone who once lived for applause begins serving where nobody sees.
These are not small things.
They are glimpses of what happens when the Gospel moves beyond our vocabulary and begins reshaping our lives.
And that is the transformation we should long for.
Not merely louder gatherings.
But deeper faith.
Not merely stronger personalities.
But healthier churches.
Not merely impressive gifts.
But lives increasingly marked by truth, love, holiness, and humility.
Not merely people who know how to respond to a preacher.
But disciples who know how to follow Jesus.
If this message exposed something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend otherwise.
You do not need to disclose private details or tell your whole story publicly.
Sometimes an honest request for prayer is enough.
Someone reading silently may need the reminder that Jesus remains faithful.
Not because we need to win an argument.
Not because every church must worship in the same style.
But because someone you know may be confusing the power of a personality with the presence of God.
Someone may be afraid to question harmful leadership.
Someone may be growing disillusioned with Christianity because they have mistaken the failures of a minister for the character of Christ.
And someone may be serving faithfully in obscurity, needing to remember that heaven's evaluation is not measured by online attention.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who is struggling, the Christian who has grown spiritually complacent, and even the seeker who is not yet sure what to believe.
There is room here for sincere questions.
There is room for conviction.
There is room for people who are still learning how to walk faithfully with Jesus.
And if this message has helped you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing biblical truth, strengthening disciples, encouraging wounded believers, and helping people move beyond inspirational moments into lasting spiritual growth.
We want those resources and messages to keep reaching people who need them.
And sustaining and expanding that work requires more than passion. It requires prayer, faithful service, time, resources, and the willing support of people who believe in the mission.
Scripture calls us to generosity without coercion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be decided in the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not from fear.
Not from guilt.
But because you may genuinely want to participate in helping this work continue and expand.
These products are simply expressions of appreciation and ways to encourage faith in everyday life. They are not the reason we preach the Gospel, and they are never a substitute for it.
It is the opportunity to help keep the message of Jesus Christ moving beyond this article, beyond this page, and into lives we may never personally meet.
Your worth before God is not measured by what you can give to this ministry.
We are grateful for every person who walks with us in faith, prayer, truth, and love.
Because ultimately, Gospel Warrior is not about building a personality-centered movement.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
The same Jesus who confronted hypocrisy without abandoning mercy.
The same Jesus who exposed sin while offering forgiveness to repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who welcomed the broken, challenged the proud, restored the fallen, and laid down His life for our redemption.
The same Jesus who rose from the grave and remains worthy of our worship.
So let the preacher preach.
Let the musician sing.
Let the congregation rejoice.
Let spiritual gifts serve the church as Scripture teaches.
Let the tears flow when hearts are genuinely moved.
But let everything be tested by God's Word.
Let leaders remain accountable.
Let truth matter more than performance.
Let the wounded be protected.
Let repentance be real.
Let grace never become a disguise for unrepentant sin.
And above everything else…
Let Jesus Christ be the One we cannot stop talking about when the service is over.
Because one day, the lights will go out.
The music will stop.
The applause will fade.
The livestream will end.
The platform will belong to someone else.
The crowd will go home.
And every human reputation will finally be seen in the light of God's perfect judgment.
On that day, the question will not be whether we were impressed by the messenger.
What matters eternally is whether we truly belong to Jesus Christ.
So do not build your faith on a voice that can fail you.
Build your life on the Savior who died and rose again.
Do not settle for being entertained by the Gospel.
Believe it.
Repent.
Receive the mercy of Christ.
Follow Him.
And let His grace transform the person you are when nobody is watching.
Because the saddest thing would not be leaving a service without feeling the fire… but spending your life applauding the messenger while never surrendering to the Savior.
